spans.text: ComputeDriven competitive benchmark — Codex stage-0 review and Fable stage-0.1 assignment
Stage 0 is a useful correctness harness, but its current performance numbers do not compare equal measurement windows or fully comparable physical cost.
The repository was clean at the reviewed commit.

The quick five-system control suite was rerun independently. All ledger/oracle, replay, conservation, starvation-visibility and arrival-time controls held across Linux, Go, BEAM, ComputeDriven and Seastar.
The whole repository guard suite passed when build output was redirected to writable scratch storage:

The adapters use the intended native scheduling shapes: Linux fair-class threads on one CPU, Go with one P, BEAM with one scheduler, Seastar with one shard and the documented 0.5 ms task quota, and the ComputeDriven policy arm with explicit residency.
Stage 0 is honest about its retained smoke being non-evidentiary.
These checks establish semantic equivalence on drain traces and show that the harness can expose starvation. They do not validate the competitive performance scorecard.
FCB-R1 — The timed window is not enforced by an independent deadline

The source writes a STOP frame at the intended deadline, but each adapter keeps counting until its own runtime schedules the reader and processes that frame. That makes the scheduler under test responsible for deciding how long it is measured.
An independent 50 ms development smoke was run on the shared host only to audit the instrument. The
closed-loop workload had a 100 ms offered interval after the common 50 ms start delay. The following work was recorded

processes ran about 741 ms and 789 ms from adapter start, even though their offered intervals differed by only 50 ms. The current marginal-instruction calculation subtracts these runs and divides by the admitted-transition delta. That slope is not a cost per transition; it includes two different, runtime-dependent overruns. The retained smoke's 623 ms Go age is explained by this same defect.

FCB-R3 — Refusal resolution is currently counted as ready-to-progress latency
excludes only mailbox admission refusals. It puts semantic
samples in the latency population even though the model defines progress as an admitted successful transition.

The audit reproduced this directly on ComputeDriven LONG: the row had 2,782 admitted transitions and 418 length refusals, while the latency population was 3,200. Resolution latency and progress latency are both useful, but they are different metrics and must be reported separately.

The current oldest-ready calculation also uses only the first sample for an event and, for closed-loop demand, the gap between every 64th sampled transition. That is not the maximum age before the next transition. Later intents in a multi-count event can wait without appearing in the age maximum, while sampled closed-loop gaps include 64 units of useful work.

Build an official runner only after C7-C9 hold. It must:
enforce the standing dedicated-host profile and fixed sentinel gates;
reject a row when source lateness exceeds a predeclared bound;
reject a whole block on a deadline, counter-domain, isolation or sentinel violation;
preserve every raw run and derive tables from them;
report confidence intervals/repeat dispersion without a synthetic score;
refuse to emit a Pareto claim when required dimensions are incomparable or missing.
Do not run that official runner in the development session.
only if all of the following hold:
C1-C9 pass with named non-vacuity mutants caught.
A short adversarial closed-loop audit shows zero post-deadline progress in all rows.
Refusal-only events appear in resolution latency and never in progress latency.
Context-switch instrumentation is nonzero on its switch-inducing control or explicitly unavailable; zero cannot silently pass.
The cross-system frontier contains only comparable dimensions.
The current ComputeDriven row is labelled as the policy adapter rather than the production kernellet.
Repository guards pass and the source tree is clean at an exact commit.
Tier B and the real-kernellet cost campaign receive separate reviews. No single winner claim combines them.

The answer to “can we benchmark now?” is split:
yes. Stage 0 is strong enough to continue.
no. The current smoke cannot rank the systems because the window and cost domains differ.
Closest path to a real comparison:
Fable completes this bounded stage-0.1 repair; Codex independently reruns C1-C9 and the window audit; then the dedicated-host Tier A campaign can be considered.
